To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) the use of implausible constraints is a major limitation of conventional approaches; and (b) the resulting bias can be avoided by using plausible prior information to relax these constraints.

(1) conventional approaches to bias correction are not applicable in nonidentified problems; (2) relaxation penalties can be derived from plausible priors; (3) the resulting models are part of a sensitivity analyses that is not a substitute for the primary analysis but rather an extension of it; and (4) the resulting inferences can be informative, even when a single model suffices to demonstrate inherent limitations.

(1) in the absence of identifying information, conventional approaches to model building and inference are not possible; (2) plausible priors are needed to relax constraints on the parameters of interest; (3) the resulting models can be fitted using familiar full or partial maximum likelihood methods; (4) the absence of identifying data renders all analyses part, not part and parcel, of a sensitivity analysis; and (5) the resulting sensitivity analysis is more powerful than conventional approaches to bias analysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing methods to make the most plausible inferences possible from nonidentified data, and to assess their sensitivity to alternative modeling assumptions.
developing and applying new statistical methods for modeling data from nonidentified sources of bias in observational studies.
developing a general framework for modeling and inference in the presence of nonidentified bias sources, and with developing and testing the associated methodology.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in observational studies, the primary goal of statistical modeling should be to identify and characterize plausible sources of bias, rather than to estimate target parameters.
the use of priors in Bayesian modeling of observational data is not only possible, but also essential to plausible modeling of bias sources.
, in the absence of identification, the only way to model nonidentified bias is to model plausible bias.
The main takeaway from our work is that
plausible priors are essential to model building when data do not identify target parameters.
plausible prior distributions are a useful tool for modeling and inference in observational studies.
the absence of identification in observational studies is a major problem that cannot be ignored.
